kept.q: Which of these materials is NOT attracted by a magnet?
kept.explanation: Iron, nickel and cobalt are ferromagnetic materials that are strongly attracted to a magnet. Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, both of which are non-magnetic, so brass is not attracted.
kept.pidgin: Iron, nickel and cobalt na magnetic materials wey magnet go pull well-well. Brass na mixture of copper and zinc, dem no be magnetic, so magnet no go pull am.

kept.q: An unmagnetized steel nail is held close to, but not touching, a strong bar magnet. After some time, the nail becomes magnetized even though it never touched the magnet. This process is called
kept.explanation: Magnetic induction is the process by which a magnetic material becomes magnetized simply by being placed near (not touching) a magnet, due to the magnet's field. Electromagnetic induction instead refers to producing an EMF/current from a changing magnetic field in a conductor.
kept.pidgin: Magnetic induction na when magnetic material dey become magnet just because e dey near another magnet, even without touch am. Electromagnetic induction na different thing, e dey talk about EMF or current wey changing field dey produce for wire.

kept.q: A coil of 200 turns is placed in a magnetic field. The magnetic flux linking the coil changes from 0.02 Wb to 0.08 Wb in 0.3 seconds. Calculate the average EMF induced in the coil, using EMF = N x (change in flux)/(time).
kept.explanation: Change in flux = 0.08 - 0.02 = 0.06 Wb. EMF = N x (delta Phi / t) = 200 x (0.06/0.3) = 200 x 0.2 = 40V.
kept.pidgin: Change in flux na 0.08 minus 0.02 = 0.06 Wb. EMF = N x (delta Phi divide t) = 200 x (0.06/0.3) = 200 x 0.2 = 40V.

kept.q: A bar magnet is pushed, north pole first, into a solenoid that is connected to a sensitive galvanometer. According to Lenz's law, the induced current that flows in the solenoid acts in a direction that
options: aids the motion of the magnet
has no effect on the magnet
moves at twice the magnet's speed
opposes the motion of the magnet
kept.explanation: Lenz's law states that the direction of an induced current is always such that it opposes the change (the motion) that produced it. So the solenoid's induced current creates a magnetic field that pushes back against the incoming magnet, opposing its motion.
kept.pidgin: Lenz's law talk say the induced current go always resist the motion wey cause am. So the solenoid go produce field wey dey push back the magnet, e no go help the magnet motion.

kept.q: A transformer has a primary coil of 1000 turns and a secondary coil of 100 turns. The primary is connected to a 240V supply and draws a current of 2A. Assuming the transformer is 100% efficient, calculate the current flowing in the secondary coil.
kept.explanation: First find secondary voltage: Vs = Vp x (Ns/Np) = 240 x (100/1000) = 24V. Since input power equals output power (100% efficient): Vp x Ip = Vs x Is, so Is = (240 x 2)/24 = 20A.
kept.pidgin: First find Vs: Vs = Vp x (Ns/Np) = 240 x (100/1000) = 24V. Since input power equal output power (100% efficient): Vp x Ip = Vs x Is, so Is = (240 x 2)/24 = 20A.

kept.q: A straight metal rod of length 0.5m moves with a velocity of 4 m/s at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.2T. Calculate the EMF induced across the ends of the rod, using EMF = B x L x v.
kept.explanation: EMF = B x L x v = 0.2 x 0.5 x 4 = 0.4V. The rod cutting across the field lines generates this motional EMF because it is moving perpendicular to the field.
kept.pidgin: EMF = B x L x v = 0.2 x 0.5 x 4 = 0.4V. The rod wey dey cut the field lines go generate this EMF because e dey move perpendicular to the field.
